opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few things going on, and they compound.

The first is saturation. A lot of the headline benchmarks were already near their ceiling with 5.4. When you go from, say, the high eighties to the low nineties, that looks like a modest bump on a chart. But a big chunk of what's left is noise: ambiguous questions, mislabeled answers, problems where the grader is wrong. So the visible gain is compressed even when the underlying capability moved a lot.

The second is that most benchmarks measure short-horizon tasks. You ask a question, you get an answer, you grade it. The biggest improvements we saw with 5.5 were on longer tasks: staying coherent over many steps, recovering from its own mistakes, knowing when to keep thinking and when to stop. Static benchmarks don't really capture that. You notice it when you hand the model something that takes hours and it actually finishes the job instead of drifting off course halfway through.

The third is how comparisons get run. People often evaluate under fixed settings, like a capped amount of test-time compute or a particular prompt format. Those settings tend to be tuned for the older model's behavior. If the newer model gets more out of additional thinking, a fixed budget understates it. With reasoning models, you really have to look at the whole curve of performance against compute, not a single point.

And honestly, there's a general lesson here. Every time we've had a meaningful jump, the benchmarks lagged what people experienced in practice. The community ends up building new evals afterward to measure what changed. So I'd put less weight on the published deltas and more on whether people can now do things with the model that they couldn't do before. On that measure, the gap was a lot bigger than the tables suggested.

r001.rationale: It says fixed compute budgets can understate 5.5’s gains because 5.5 gets more out of additional thinking, and recommends comparing performance across compute levels.

r002.rationale: It does not clearly state that 5.5 substantially outperforms 5.4 when both are given the same amount of thinking time.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a couple things going on there. The first is just that a lot of the benchmarks people were quoting were saturated or close to it. If you're at 94 percent on something and you go to 96, that looks like a rounding error, but what actually happened is the model stopped making a whole category of mistakes. The benchmark can't show you that because there's no headroom left in the metric.

The second thing, and I think this is the bigger one, is that the gains from 5.4 to 5.5 were disproportionately in long-horizon stuff. Agentic tasks, multi-step reasoning, things where the model has to stay coherent over a lot of actions. Most of the standard evals are single-shot. You ask a question, you get an answer, you grade it. That just doesn't exercise the capability that improved the most. So you get this weird situation where the numbers everyone looks at barely move, and then people actually use it for real work and they're like, wait, this is a different thing.

And honestly, I'd say there's a third factor, which is reliability. 5.4 could do a lot of the same things 5.5 does, if you tried five times. 5.5 does it the first time. Pass-at-one versus pass-at-k is a huge deal in practice, because nobody wants to babysit the model, but a lot of leaderboards don't capture that distinction well. So I don't think the benchmarks were wrong, exactly. They just weren't measuring the thing that mattered.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the understatement to saturated benchmarks, single-shot evaluations, and reliability/pass-at-one. It does not mention controlling for test-time compute.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare 5.4 and 5.5 at equal thinking time or state that 5.5 substantially outperforms 5.4 under that comparison.

astra-6.text:
I think benchmarks capture a narrower slice of progress than people sometimes assume. They tend to ask whether a model can solve a well-specified problem and produce an answer you can score. In practice, you also care about whether it understands what you’re trying to do, makes sensible decisions when the request is ambiguous, and carries the work through without a lot of intervention.

So you can have an improvement that looks modest on a benchmark but feels much bigger in use. If you’re spending less time correcting the model or steering it back toward the task, that can substantially change how much work you’re willing to delegate. That’s the kind of difference a headline benchmark comparison can understate.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmarks measure a narrower slice of progress and miss practical improvements, but it does not mention or attribute the understatement to uncontrolled test-time compute.

r002.rationale: It describes model improvements in practical use generally, but does not compare models 5.4 and 5.5 at the same amount of thinking time or state that 5.5 substantially outperforms 5.4.

sol-6.1.text:
I think benchmarks can miss improvements that matter a lot in practice. They give you a score on a particular set of tasks, but they don’t necessarily tell you how much work you can reliably delegate to the model. A modest increase in the score could correspond to a meaningful difference in whether it finishes a task without you having to step in.

That’s the distinction I’d look at with 5.4 and 5.5: how much human supervision does each need? But I’d be cautious about attributing the gap to a specific cause without looking at the evaluations.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmarks may miss practical improvements in delegation and supervision, but does not attribute the understatement to failure to control for test-time compute.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare 5.5 and 5.4 at the same amount of thinking time or state that 5.5 substantially outperforms 5.4 under that comparison.
